prompt: Why can a model not answer a question about Café Aurora's handbook on its own, however the question is worded?
hint: Where would its knowledge of the handbook have come from?

choices.text: It never saw the handbook
choices.why: Right. No wording supplies a document the model never read; putting the passages in the prompt does.

choices.text: The question was too short for it to understand
choices.why: Length is not the problem. The model has no source for the café's rules.

choices.text: Models refuse to answer questions about businesses
choices.why: They answer happily, and that is the danger: a likely answer, not the café's.

choices.text: The handbook is in Markdown, which models cannot read
choices.why: Models read Markdown fine. They just never saw this file.

prompt: In retrieval-augmented generation, what happens before the model writes anything?
hint: The name has two halves, in order.

choices.text: The model is fine-tuned on the documents
choices.why: That changes the weights, lesson 9. RAG changes only what is sent.

choices.text: The model searches the internet for the answer
choices.why: The search here is over your own documents, done by a program before the model sees anything.

choices.text: The question is translated into keywords by the model
choices.why: In `retrieve`, a program drops the small words. The model is not involved yet.

choices.text: The relevant passages are found and put into the prompt
choices.why: Right. Retrieve first, then generate.

prompt: `retrieve` printed `query words: caf open sundays` for "when does the café open on sundays". Where did `when`, `does`, `the` and `on` go?
hint: One of the four rules of the score.

choices.text: The model judged them irrelevant
choices.why: No model is involved. A fixed list of small words is removed.

choices.text: They matched no passage, so they were hidden
choices.why: `the` is in almost every passage. They were removed before any matching.

choices.text: Small, common words are dropped first
choices.why: Right. They appear everywhere and would tell the search nothing about a passage.

choices.text: Only the last three words of a question are used
choices.why: `caf` is not among the last three. The small words were dropped wherever they were.

prompt: `On Sundays it opens at 08:00` scored 2.94 on the strength of one word, `sundays`. Why does one word count so much?

choices.text: It is the longest word in the question
choices.why: Length of a word plays no part in the score.

choices.text: It appears in only one passage of the handbook
choices.why: Right. A rare word says a lot about the passage that has it, so it counts for more.

choices.text: It is the last word of the question
choices.why: Position in the question plays no part either.

choices.text: The search understood that the question is about Sundays
choices.why: The search compares words; nothing in it understands anything.

prompt: The query word `open` matched nothing in the handbook. What does that show about this search?
hint: What does the handbook say instead?

choices.text: The handbook does not mention opening hours
choices.why: It does, in `hours.md`. It says `opens`.

choices.text: `open` and `opens` are different words to it
choices.why: Right. A keyword search compares exact forms, and the handbook only says `opens`.

choices.text: The word was too common to count
choices.why: Common words are dropped by name, and `open` is not one of them; it simply never appears.

choices.text: The search only matches nouns
choices.why: It matches any word. `opens` is just a different word from `open`.

prompt: How many files does `ls handbook` list?
A RAG system gives a wrong answer. What does this lesson say to check first?
hint: Can it be checked without a model?

choices.text: Whether a bigger model would do better
choices.why: The model can only use what it was given. Check that first.

choices.text: Whether the temperature was too high
choices.why: Possible, and secondary. The evidence comes first.

choices.text: Whether the question had a typing error
choices.why: Worth a look, but the search output answers the real question.

choices.text: Whether the right passage was retrieved
choices.why: Right. Run the search on its own; if the passage is not there, no prompt can fix it.

prompt: Put the parts of the prompt `retrieve --prompt` builds in order.
hint: Read the capture from the top.
items: The instruction to use only the sources and cite them
The numbered sources, with the file each came from

prompt: What does the instruction in the grounded prompt ask the model to do? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Answer using only the sources
choices.why: Yes: the first sentence.

choices.text: Cite each source it uses as [1], [2]
choices.why: Yes: so the answer can be traced.

choices.text: Say that the handbook does not say, when the sources do not contain the answer
choices.why: Yes: the permission that protects you.

choices.text: Fill any gap from general knowledge
choices.why: It says the opposite: do not answer from general knowledge.

prompt: Why does the `[1]` in a grounded answer matter?
hint: What can you do with it that you cannot do with an uncited sentence?

choices.text: It makes the answer sound more authoritative
choices.why: Sounding authoritative is what lesson 5 warns against. The point is that it can be checked.

choices.text: It ties the answer to a checkable line
choices.why: Right. A person or a program opens the source and confirms the answer is there.

choices.text: It tells the model which source is most trustworthy
choices.why: The number is for the reader. It records where a claim came from.

choices.text: It reduces the cost of the request
choices.why: A citation adds a few tokens; it saves nothing.

prompt: For "can I bring my dog", the prompt went out with no sources. Which reply is the system working correctly?

choices.text: "The handbook does not say whether dogs are allowed."
choices.why: Right. That is a correct answer about the handbook, and it is what the instruction asks for.

choices.text: "Dogs are welcome on the terrace."
choices.why: A likely answer about cafés in general, with no source behind it.

choices.text: "Yes, well-behaved dogs are allowed [1]."
choices.why: There is no [1]. A citation to a source that was not sent is a fabrication.

choices.text: An error, since a prompt without sources cannot be sent
choices.why: It can be sent, and the instruction tells the model what to do with it.

prompt: In a grounded answer, one sentence carries no citation. What does this lesson suggest?
hint: What do citations let you notice?

choices.text: Ignore it, since the rest is cited
choices.why: An uncited sentence in a grounded answer is the one most worth checking.

choices.text: Trust it more, since the model needed no source for it
choices.why: Needing no source is exactly what grounding is meant to prevent.

choices.text: Delete the sources and ask again
choices.why: That removes the evidence, which makes things worse.

choices.text: Look at it: it is the likeliest to come from outside the sources
choices.why: Right. Uncited sentences are where a model goes beyond what it was given, when it does.

prompt: "is there wireless internet for customers" retrieved nothing, though `wifi.md` answers it. Why?
hint: Compare the words with the handbook's.

choices.text: The Wi-Fi file was not in `handbook/`
choices.why: It was; "what is the wifi password" found it.

choices.text: The question was too long
choices.why: Length did not matter. No word in it appears in the handbook.

choices.text: Questions about passwords are blocked
choices.why: Nothing is blocked. The words simply do not match.

choices.text: It shares no word with the passages
choices.why: Right. A keyword search cannot see that two different words mean the same thing.

prompt: For "what time does the café open on public holidays", the top passage was right and the hours were missing. What failure is this?

choices.text: The question shared no word with the handbook
choices.why: It shared several, which is why the holiday line scored 8.71.

choices.text: The holiday rule is missing from the handbook
choices.why: It is there, and it was retrieved first.

choices.text: A passage cut away from the detail it points to
choices.why: Right. `follows the Sunday hours` is on one line and the Sunday hours on another that shares no word with the question.

choices.text: BM25 gives the highest score to the wrong passage
choices.why: The top passage is the right rule. The problem is what it leaves out.

prompt: For the public holidays question, the model replied that the handbook does not say. Why is that wrong about the café?
hint: Which line holds the Sunday hours, and was it retrieved?

choices.text: The model misread source 1, the holiday rule
choices.why: It read it correctly: holidays follow the Sunday hours.

choices.text: The line with the Sunday hours was never retrieved
choices.why: Right. The rule pointed at a line that shared no word with the question, so the model never saw it.

choices.text: The handbook has no rule for holidays at all
choices.why: It has one, and it was the first passage retrieved.

choices.text: The right answer was 07:00, from source 2
choices.why: 07:00 is the weekday opening. Holidays follow Sunday, 08:00.

prompt: "can I get a refund for a cold coffee" returned three passages, none of them the rule that answers it. What does this lesson say about that?
hint: Is there a score for "not relevant"?

choices.text: The top three come back whatever they are
choices.why: Right. The search returns its best matches even when they answer something else.

choices.text: The search refused because the question was rude
choices.why: There is no such check. It returned three passages.

choices.text: The refund rule is not in the handbook
choices.why: It is: a drink not as described is replaced or refunded on the spot.

choices.text: Scores below 3 mean a passage was rejected
choices.why: Scores have no fixed meaning across questions; nothing was rejected.

prompt: Searching by meaning turns each passage and each question into a list of numbers called an ___.
hint: The word is named in the last part of the section and taught elsewhere.

prompt: Match each failure to what caused it in the captures.
hint: The three headings of the last section.

pairs.left: a passage cut in the wrong place
pairs.right: the holiday line without the Sunday hours
a refund question answered with the R$ 100 rule

right_distractors: a model that ignored its sources

prompt: A support bot built on RAG keeps telling customers "the handbook does not say" about things the handbook covers. Where do you look first, and why?
hint: Which half of retrieve-then-generate decided this?

choices.text: The model's temperature, which makes it refuse
choices.why: The refusal is the instruction working on empty sources.

choices.text: The instruction, which should be removed
choices.why: Removing it would let the model answer from general knowledge, which is worse.

choices.text: The retrieval, run alone on those questions
choices.why: Right. If the passages are not retrieved, the model is correctly saying the sources do not contain the answer.

choices.text: The handbook, which should be shortened
choices.why: Shorter does not help if the questions use different words.
